state.misconception_label: Ignores negative sign when expanding bracket

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: John is expanding these three brackets: \( (x+5)(x-3)(x+6) \) He finds it helpful to split the first bracket and view the problem as follows: \( x(x-3)(x+6)+5(x-3)(x+6) \) He expands the brackets further. Before he simplifies, what are the terms than contain an \( \boldsymbol{x}^{2} \) ? I got \( \begin{array}{l}+6 x^{2} \\ +3 x^{2} \\ +5 x^{2}\end{array} \) because I forgot that two negatives multiply to a positive.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's focus on the misconception you mentioned about two negatives multiplying to a positive. Remember, when expanding brackets, we need to carefully consider the signs of the terms. Can you explain why two negatives multiply to a positive in this context?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get it a bit better now. So when I have \( (x-3) \) and I multiply it by another negative, like when I expand \( (x+5)(x-3) \), it should actually be positive, right? But I'm still confused about how to keep track of the signs when I'm expanding all the brackets together. Can you help me with that?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's focus on keeping track of the signs when expanding all the brackets together. Remember, when you have a negative sign in front of a term, it affects the sign of that term when multiplied. Can you try expanding the brackets again, paying close attention to the signs as you go along?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I’ll try again. So when I expand \( (x+5)(x-3) \), I should remember that the \(-3\) makes the \(5\) negative when I multiply it, right? But then when I do \( (x-3)(x+6) \), I get confused about how the negative affects the \(x\) terms. Can you show me how to keep track of the signs better when I expand all the brackets together?
